title: Setting up your development environment
notes: Use Python 3.11 or newer, with one virtual environment per project so its packages stay separate.
Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in code, and never commit it to Git.
A model call is a client, the messages create method and the text block from the reply; keep a messages list and you have a chatbot that remembers.

slides.title: Setting up your development environment
slides.sub: Python, a virtual environment, an API key and your first model call
sentences: Time to put your hands on the keyboard.
In this lesson you will see everything Scout needs: Python, a project folder, the Anthropic SDK and an API key.
Then you will see your first call to a model, in about ten lines of code.
Right after this video, the guided practice walks you through every step on your own machine.

slides.title: What you need
slides.lead: Four things. The tools are free; only the model calls cost money.

bullets.text: A code editor, such as VS Code, and a terminal
An Anthropic account and an API key from the console
A little API credit: this module's calls cost a few cents

aside.label: Never coded?
aside.text: That's fine. Every command and file is given in full: you copy, run and read the result.

sentences: Here is what you need before you start.
Python, version three point eleven or newer, which you can check from the terminal.
A code editor, such as VS Code, and a terminal window to run commands.
An Anthropic account, where you create an API key: a secret code that lets your programs use the model.
And a little API credit, because model calls are paid, though everything in this module costs a few cents.
If you have never written code before, that's fine: every command and file is given in full.

slides.title: A folder and a virtual environment
slides.lead: A virtual environment is a private set of Python packages for one project.

rows.out: turns it on in Windows PowerShell
turns it on in macOS or Linux

aside.label: How to tell
aside.text: When it's active, your prompt starts with (.venv). Activate it again in every new terminal.

sentences: Everything for Scout lives in one folder, called scout.
Inside it, you make a virtual environment: a private set of Python packages for this project only, so projects never clash.
You create it once, with a tool that comes built into Python.
Then you activate it, with one command on Windows and a slightly different one on Mac or Linux.
With it active, pip install anthropic adds Anthropic's official SDK, the library your code uses to talk to the model.
You can tell it's active because its name appears in brackets at the start of your terminal prompt.
Activate it again every time you open a new terminal.

slides.title: Where your API key lives

right.label: In an environment variable
points: The SDK finds it by itself
Your code is safe to share

sentences: Your API key works like a password with your payment card attached, so where you keep it matters.
Never paste it into your code.
Code gets shared, copied and pushed to GitHub, and automated scanners search public code for leaked keys.
Anyone who finds your key can spend your credit until you delete it.
Instead, put it in an environment variable: a named value your terminal holds for programs to read.
The SDK looks for a variable called Anthropic API key, so your code never contains the key at all.
Add a git ignore file too, so the virtual environment and any secrets file are never committed.

slides.title: Setting the key
slides.lead: Run one line in the terminal where you'll run Scout, with your own key in place of the dots.

rows.out: the SDK reads the key by itself

aside.label: Only this terminal
aside.text: A key set this way lasts until you close the terminal. Set it again in each new one.

sentences: Setting the key takes one line in the terminal.
On Windows, you set it in PowerShell.
On Mac or Linux, you use the export command instead.
Then, in Python, creating the client is enough: the SDK finds the key in the environment by itself.
One catch: a key set like this lasts only until you close that terminal, so set it again in each new one.
The guided practice also shows you how to make it permanent.

slides.title: Your first model call
slides.lead: hello.py sends one message to the model and prints the reply.

rows.out: calls the model: model, max_tokens, messages

rows.code: next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
rows.out: picks the text block out of the reply

aside.label: max_tokens=16000
aside.text: A ceiling on the reply's length, not a target. Short questions still get short answers.

sentences: Here is your first model call, in a small script named hello.
First, the script creates a client and names the model; this course uses Claude Opus five point five.
Then it calls the messages create method with the model, a maximum length, and the conversation so far.
Here the conversation is just one user message: a question about AI agents.
Finally, it picks the text block out of the reply and prints it.
The maximum tokens setting is a ceiling, not a target, so short questions still get short answers.

slides.title: What happens when you run it

note.text: One model call, not an agent yet: no tools and no loop. It can talk, but it can't act.

sentences: Let's follow that call from start to finish.
Your script builds the request, with the model name and your message.
The SDK attaches your API key and sends the request over the internet to Anthropic's API.
The model reads the message, may think it through first, and writes its answer.
The reply comes back as a list of content blocks, which is why you pick out the block whose type is text.
Your script prints it, and the answer appears in your terminal.
That is one model call, not an agent yet: there are no tools and no loop, so it can talk, but it can't act.

slides.title: From one call to a chatbot

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Hi Ana! How can I help with your gear today?

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: I'm sorry, I can't look up orders. Your confirmation email should have the details.

aside.label: Sound familiar?
aside.text: Scout remembers and talks, but can't look anything up. That's Orbit's problem, and Module 3 fixes it.

sentences: In the guided practice, you will turn that single call into a small chatbot that runs in your terminal.
It keeps a list of messages, adding your turn and the model's reply each time round.
Because the whole list is sent with every call, it remembers that your name is Ana.
The model itself remembers nothing between calls; the list is the memory.
Then you ask it about a real order, with the order number.
It can't know: there is no orders system anywhere in your code, so the best it can do is apologise.
That is Orbit's chatbot problem, recreated on your own machine, and it is exactly what the next modules fix.

anthropic installed; the API key in an environment variable, never in Git
A model call: client, messages.create, then the text block
A messages list turns one call into a chatbot that remembers

sentences: Here is your checklist.
Python three point eleven or newer, a scout folder, and a virtual environment that you activate in every new terminal.
The Anthropic SDK installed with pip, and your API key in an environment variable, never in code and never in Git.
A model call is a client, the messages create method, and the text block from the reply.
Keep a list of messages, and your chatbot remembers the conversation.
Now open your terminal: the guided practice walks you through every step.

midQuiz.q: Why give the scout project its own virtual environment?
options: It keeps this project's packages separate from everything else
It stores your API key safely
midQuiz.explain: A virtual environment is a private set of packages for one project, so installing or upgrading things for Scout never breaks another project.
midQuiz.hint: Think about where pip install puts the packages.

midQuiz.q: Where should your Anthropic API key live?
options: In hello.py, so it's easy to find
In an environment variable that the SDK reads
In a comment at the top of chat.py
midQuiz.explain: The SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment, so the key never appears in your files and can't be committed by accident.
midQuiz.hint: Which option keeps the key out of every file you might share?

endQuiz.q: A reply holds two content blocks: thinking, then text. How does hello.py get the answer?
options: It takes the first block whose type is text
It prints the whole response object
endQuiz.explain: The first block may be the model's thinking. next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text") picks the text block, wherever it is.
endQuiz.hint: Which approach still works if the text isn't the first block?

endQuiz.q: chat.py remembers that you're Ana. Why?
options: The model stores every conversation on Anthropic's servers
The script sends the whole messages list with every call
The API key links all your calls together
endQuiz.explain: The model remembers nothing between calls. chat.py appends each turn to the messages list and sends the whole list every time.
endQuiz.hint: What does chat.py add to after every turn?
